name.text: What the TDD Rules Explorer does

questiontext.text: What does the TDD Rules Explorer let you do?

answer.text: Apply TDD actions one at a time; illegal moves are blocked and the violated discipline rule is explained

feedback.text: Correct — you try actions and the explorer enforces the TDD discipline rules, explaining any blocked move.

answer.text: Automatically play through the red-green-refactor phases with no input from you

feedback.text: That is a passive walkthrough; the Rules Explorer is interactive and enforces which moves are legal.

answer.text: Measure how much of the production code the test suite covers

feedback.text: That is code coverage; the Rules Explorer enforces TDD discipline rules, not coverage metrics.

answer.text: Generate production code automatically from a written test

feedback.text: It does not generate code; it checks whether each action you take obeys the TDD rules.

generalfeedback.text: The TDD Rules Explorer lets you apply TDD actions one at a time. When an action would break a discipline rule it is blocked and the explorer names the rule that was violated, so you learn the rules by seeing which move each one forbids.

name.text: When production code may be written

questiontext.text: According to the rules, when may you write production code?

answer.text: Only when there is a failing test

feedback.text: Correct — production code may be written only to make a failing test pass.

answer.text: At any time, whenever you feel like adding code

feedback.text: No — production code always needs a failing test to justify it first.

answer.text: Only when all tests are already passing

feedback.text: If all tests pass there is nothing failing to drive the code; you need a failing test first.

answer.text: Only immediately after a refactor

feedback.text: Refactoring does not authorise new production code; a failing test does.

generalfeedback.text: The most fundamental rule: you may not write production code without a failing test. The explorer blocks a "write production code" move whenever there is no failing test, telling you to write a failing test first.

name.text: Writing code with no failing test

questiontext.text: You write production code while no test is failing. Which rule does this break?

answer.text: You may not write production code without a failing test — write a failing test first

feedback.text: Correct — production code must be justified by a failing test.

answer.text: You may not write two tests in a row

feedback.text: That is not the rule here; the broken rule is writing production code with no failing test.

answer.text: You may not refactor while a test is failing

feedback.text: That rule is about refactoring; here the problem is code written with no failing test.

answer.text: No rule is broken; this is always allowed

feedback.text: It is blocked: production code requires a failing test to justify it.

generalfeedback.text: Writing production code with nothing failing violates the rule "you may not write production code without a failing test." The explorer blocks the move and tells you to write a failing test first.

name.text: When a new failing test may be written

questiontext.text: According to the rules, when may you write a new failing test?

answer.text: Only when you do not already have a failing test — make the current one pass first

feedback.text: Correct — you may not stack a second failing test on top of an unpassed one.

answer.text: At any time, even with a test already failing

feedback.text: No — if a test is already failing you must make it pass before writing another.

answer.text: Only after refactoring the production code

feedback.text: Refactoring is not a precondition; you just need no test currently failing.

answer.text: Only when the cycle count is zero

feedback.text: You can start new tests in later cycles too; the condition is that no test is currently failing.

generalfeedback.text: You may write a failing test only when you do not already have one. If a failing test exists, the rule requires you to make it pass before writing another, keeping you focused on one behaviour at a time.

name.text: Writing a second failing test

questiontext.text: A test is currently failing, and you try to write another failing test. Does this obey or break a rule?

answer.text: It breaks a rule — you already have a failing test, so make it pass before writing another

feedback.text: Correct — only one failing test at a time; make it pass first.

answer.text: It obeys the rules — you may have as many failing tests as you like

feedback.text: No — the rule permits only one failing test at a time.

answer.text: It obeys the rules only if the tests are unrelated

feedback.text: The rule does not depend on relatedness; a test is already failing, so this is blocked.

answer.text: It breaks the rule about refactoring while red

feedback.text: Wrong rule — this concerns writing a second failing test, not refactoring.

generalfeedback.text: The explorer blocks this move: "you already have a failing test. Make it pass before writing another." The discipline keeps you working on a single failing test at a time.

name.text: No refactoring while a test is failing

questiontext.text: Under the rules, you may not refactor while a test is failing.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — you must get to green before refactoring.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Refactoring while red is blocked; the rule says get to green first.

generalfeedback.text: Refactoring is only safe when the tests are green, because green tests are the safety net that proves behaviour is preserved. The explorer blocks a refactor while a test is failing and tells you to get to green first.

name.text: When refactoring is allowed

questiontext.text: According to the rules, when is refactoring allowed?

answer.text: Only when all tests pass, none is failing, and at least one red-green cycle is complete

feedback.text: Correct — refactor from green, with something actually built to refactor.

answer.text: At any time, including before any test is written

feedback.text: No — refactoring needs green tests and at least one completed cycle first.

answer.text: Only while a test is failing, so you can fix it

feedback.text: Fixing a failing test is writing production code; refactoring requires green.

answer.text: Only before writing any production code

feedback.text: There is nothing to refactor before production code exists; you need a completed cycle.

generalfeedback.text: Refactoring is legal only from a green state: all tests pass, none is failing, and at least one red-green cycle has produced code worth cleaning up. Otherwise the explorer blocks the move.

name.text: The only legal first move

questiontext.text: At the very start (nothing written yet), which action is legal?

answer.text: Write a failing test

feedback.text: Correct — the only legal opening move is to write a failing test.

answer.text: Write production code

feedback.text: Blocked — there is no failing test yet to justify production code.

answer.text: Refactor

feedback.text: Blocked — there is nothing built yet to refactor.

answer.text: Any of the three actions is equally legal

feedback.text: Only writing a failing test is legal at the start; the other two are blocked.

generalfeedback.text: From the initial state there is no failing test and no completed cycle, so writing production code and refactoring are both blocked. The only legal opening move is to write a failing test.

name.text: Starting with a failing test obeys the rules

questiontext.text: From a fresh start you write a failing test first. Does this obey the rules?

answer.text: Yes — writing a failing test is the legal opening move

feedback.text: Correct — this is exactly how a TDD cycle is meant to begin.

answer.text: No — you should write the production code first

feedback.text: Production code first is blocked; the failing test comes first.

answer.text: No — you should refactor first

feedback.text: There is nothing to refactor at the start; the failing test comes first.

answer.text: Only if a previous cycle already exists

feedback.text: No prior cycle is needed; a failing test is legal from the very start.

generalfeedback.text: Writing a failing test first obeys the rules and is the intended opening of a TDD cycle. It sets up the failing test that then justifies writing production code.

name.text: Meaning of the "Has failing test" field

questiontext.text: In the explorer's state panel, what does Has failing test indicate?

answer.text: That a written test is currently not yet passing

feedback.text: Correct — it flags an unpassed (red) test.

answer.text: That the production code failed to compile

feedback.text: The field tracks an unpassed test, not compilation status.

answer.text: The total number of tests ever written

feedback.text: It is a yes/no flag for a currently-failing test, not a count.

answer.text: That the last refactor introduced a bug

feedback.text: It simply marks whether a written test is not yet passing.

generalfeedback.text: "Has failing test" is true when a written test is not yet passing. It is the flag the rules check: it must be true to write production code, and false to write a new failing test or to refactor.

name.text: Meaning of the "All green" field

questiontext.text: In the state panel, what does All green mean?

answer.text: Every written test passes (it is vacuously true at the start, when none exist)

feedback.text: Correct — all green means no test is currently failing.

answer.text: The user interface is using a green colour theme

feedback.text: It refers to test status, not the visual theme.

answer.text: The production code compiled successfully

feedback.text: It is about tests passing, not compilation.

answer.text: At least one test has been written

feedback.text: It means every written test passes; at the start it is true even though none exist.

generalfeedback.text: "All green" is true when every written test passes. At the start it is vacuously true because there are no failing tests. Refactoring requires this to be true (plus a completed cycle).

name.text: Meaning of "Cycles completed"

questiontext.text: In the state panel, what does Cycles completed count?

answer.text: The number of completed red-to-green cycles

feedback.text: Correct — it counts how many times a failing test was driven to passing.

answer.text: The number of refactorings performed

feedback.text: Refactoring does not advance this count; completing red-to-green does.

answer.text: The number of tests currently failing

feedback.text: That is a different field; this counts completed red-to-green cycles.

answer.text: The number of lines of production code written

feedback.text: It counts completed cycles, not lines of code.

generalfeedback.text: "Cycles completed" counts completed red-to-green cycles — each time you take a failing test to passing. It must be at least one before refactoring is allowed, because otherwise there is nothing built to refactor.

name.text: Refactoring at the very start is blocked

questiontext.text: At the very start, with nothing written, you try to refactor and it is blocked. What is the reason?

answer.text: Nothing to refactor yet — complete at least one red-green cycle first

feedback.text: Correct — there is no code produced yet, so there is nothing to clean up.

answer.text: A test is currently failing

feedback.text: No test is failing at the start; the reason is that nothing has been built yet.

answer.text: You must write production code before refactoring

feedback.text: The precise reason the explorer gives is that no cycle is complete yet, so there is nothing to refactor.

answer.text: Refactoring is never allowed in TDD

feedback.text: Refactoring is allowed from green after a cycle; at the start there is simply nothing to refactor.

generalfeedback.text: At the start all tests are (vacuously) green, but no cycle is complete, so the explorer blocks refactoring with "nothing to refactor yet — complete at least one red-green cycle first."

name.text: Only legal move after a failing test

questiontext.text: Right after you write a failing test, the only legal next action is to write production code (to make it pass).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — with a test failing, you cannot write another test or refactor; you must write production code.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: With a test failing, writing another failing test and refactoring are both blocked, so only writing production code is legal.

generalfeedback.text: After writing a failing test the state has a failing test and is not all green. Writing another failing test is blocked (one at a time) and refactoring is blocked (not green), so the only legal move is to write production code.

name.text: What the explorer does with an illegal move

questiontext.text: When you attempt an illegal move, what does the explorer do?

answer.text: Blocks the move, leaves the state unchanged, and explains the violated rule

feedback.text: Correct — an illegal move is refused and the broken rule is named.

answer.text: Applies the move anyway but shows a warning

feedback.text: No — the move is blocked and the state is left unchanged.

answer.text: Resets the whole explorer to the start

feedback.text: It does not reset; it just blocks the illegal move and explains why.

answer.text: Silently ignores the click with no feedback

feedback.text: It gives feedback — it explains which discipline rule the move would break.

generalfeedback.text: An illegal move is blocked: the state does not change and the explorer shows which discipline rule the move would have violated. A legal move, by contrast, is applied and the state advances.

name.text: Scenario: implementing before any test

questiontext.text: A developer starts a new class and immediately writes its implementation before writing any test. Which rule is broken?

answer.text: You may not write production code without a failing test

feedback.text: Correct — code written with no failing test violates the first rule.

answer.text: You may not have two failing tests at once

feedback.text: No test exists here at all; the broken rule is writing code with no failing test.

answer.text: You may not refactor while red

feedback.text: Nothing is being refactored; the issue is production code with no failing test.

answer.text: You may not complete more than one cycle per test

feedback.text: That is not a rule; the violation is writing code before any failing test.

generalfeedback.text: Writing the implementation before any test means there is no failing test to justify it, breaking "you may not write production code without a failing test." A failing test must come first.

name.text: Scenario: piling on a second failing test

questiontext.text: A developer has one test failing and, before making it pass, writes a second failing test. Which rule is broken?

answer.text: You already have a failing test — make it pass before writing another

feedback.text: Correct — only one failing test at a time.

answer.text: You may not write production code without a failing test

feedback.text: That rule concerns production code; here a second failing test was added.

answer.text: You may not refactor while a test is failing

feedback.text: No refactoring is happening; the issue is a second failing test.

answer.text: You may not refactor before a cycle completes

feedback.text: Wrong rule — this is about adding a second failing test, not refactoring.

generalfeedback.text: Adding a second failing test before resolving the first breaks the rule "you already have a failing test. Make it pass before writing another." The discipline keeps you on one behaviour at a time.

name.text: Scenario: cleaning up while red

questiontext.text: A test is currently failing and the developer starts tidying up (refactoring) the code. Which rule is broken?

answer.text: You may not refactor while a test is failing — get to green first

feedback.text: Correct — refactoring needs a green safety net.

answer.text: You may not write production code without a failing test

feedback.text: There is a failing test here; the broken rule is refactoring while red.

answer.text: You already have a failing test, so you cannot write another

feedback.text: No new test is being written; the issue is refactoring while a test is failing.

answer.text: Nothing to refactor yet

feedback.text: That reason applies before any cycle; here the block is because a test is failing.

generalfeedback.text: Refactoring while a test is red breaks "you may not refactor while a test is failing. Get to green first." Only green tests can prove that a refactor preserved behaviour.

name.text: Scenario: refactoring on a brand-new project

questiontext.text: On a brand-new project with nothing written, a developer tries to refactor. Which reason blocks the move?

answer.text: Nothing to refactor yet — complete at least one red-green cycle first

feedback.text: Correct — with no completed cycle there is nothing to clean up.

answer.text: A test is currently failing

feedback.text: No test is failing on a brand-new project; the reason is that nothing has been built.

answer.text: Production code exists without a failing test

feedback.text: No production code exists yet; the reason is that no cycle is complete.

answer.text: Two tests are failing at once

feedback.text: No tests exist; the block is that there is nothing to refactor yet.

generalfeedback.text: Even though all tests are vacuously green at the start, no red-green cycle is complete, so there is literally nothing built to refactor. The explorer blocks with "nothing to refactor yet — complete at least one red-green cycle first."

name.text: Consequence: every line of code is justified

questiontext.text: Because production code may be written only to pass a failing test, what does the rule force?

answer.text: Every piece of production code is justified by a test that demanded it

feedback.text: Correct — no code exists without a test that required it.

answer.text: Production code can be added speculatively for future needs

feedback.text: The opposite — speculative code has no failing test to justify it, so it is forbidden.

answer.text: Tests become optional once the design is clear

feedback.text: Tests are never optional here; they are what authorise the code.

answer.text: The whole feature must be coded before any test runs

feedback.text: That inverts the rule; a failing test must precede the code.

generalfeedback.text: Requiring a failing test before production code means each piece of code exists to satisfy a specific test. Speculative, untested code has no justification, so the rule steers you toward minimal, demand-driven code.

name.text: Consequence: tiny increments

questiontext.text: Because you must make the current failing test pass before writing another, what discipline results?

answer.text: You work in tiny increments — one small failing test, make it pass, then repeat

feedback.text: Correct — the one-at-a-time rule enforces small steps.

answer.text: You batch many failing tests and fix them all at the end

feedback.text: That is exactly what the one-at-a-time rule forbids.

answer.text: You may skip tests when the change is small

feedback.text: No — each increment still starts from a failing test.

answer.text: You must refactor between every keystroke

feedback.text: Refactoring is optional and only from green; the rule here is about small increments.

generalfeedback.text: Allowing only one failing test at a time forces small increments: write one failing test, make it pass, and only then move on. Each step is a small, verified advance rather than a large risky leap.

name.text: Match: precondition for production code

questiontext.text: "Write production code" is legal only when ___.

answer.text: there is a failing test

feedback.text: Correct — production code is written to make a failing test pass.

answer.text: all tests are green

feedback.text: If everything is green there is nothing failing to drive the code.

answer.text: at least one cycle is complete

feedback.text: That is the precondition for refactoring, not for writing production code.

answer.text: you have just refactored

feedback.text: Refactoring does not authorise production code; a failing test does.

generalfeedback.text: Production code is a legal move only when a failing test exists to justify it. That is the direct match for the rule "you may not write production code without a failing test."

name.text: Match: precondition for refactoring

questiontext.text: "Refactor" is legal only when ___.

answer.text: all tests pass, none is failing, and at least one red-green cycle is complete

feedback.text: Correct — refactor from green, with something already built.

answer.text: a test is currently failing

feedback.text: Refactoring while red is blocked; you must be green first.

answer.text: no test has been written yet

feedback.text: With nothing written there is nothing to refactor.

answer.text: you are about to write your first test

feedback.text: Refactoring needs a completed cycle; the first test has not even produced code yet.

generalfeedback.text: Refactoring is legal only from a green state that also has at least one completed red-green cycle, so there is passing, tested code worth cleaning up while the tests guard behaviour.

name.text: Scenario: refactoring from green is legal

questiontext.text: After completing one red-green cycle, all tests pass and none is failing. The developer refactors. Is this legal?

answer.text: Yes — all tests are green and a cycle is complete, so refactoring is allowed

feedback.text: Correct — this is precisely when refactoring is permitted.

answer.text: No — you must write another failing test before refactoring

feedback.text: A new failing test is not required; green plus a completed cycle is enough.

answer.text: No — refactoring is never legal in this model

feedback.text: Refactoring is legal from green after a cycle; it is one of the three actions.

answer.text: Only if the cycle count is exactly zero

feedback.text: The count must be at least one; a completed cycle is required.

generalfeedback.text: Green tests and at least one completed cycle satisfy the refactoring rule, so the move is legal. This is the intended moment to improve the code's structure while the tests hold behaviour steady.

name.text: Scenario: starting the next cycle from green

questiontext.text: All tests are green after one completed cycle. The developer writes a new failing test. Is this legal?

answer.text: Yes — no test is currently failing, so a new failing test starts the next cycle

feedback.text: Correct — from green you may begin the next cycle with a fresh failing test.

answer.text: No — you must refactor before writing any new test

feedback.text: Refactoring is optional; you may go straight to a new failing test.

answer.text: No — a new test may only be written in the first cycle

feedback.text: New failing tests are legal in later cycles too, as long as none is currently failing.

answer.text: Only if you first write more production code

feedback.text: Production code needs a failing test; from green the legal opening is a new failing test.

generalfeedback.text: From a green state with no failing test, writing a new failing test is legal and begins the next red-green cycle. Refactoring is also legal there, but writing production code is not, because nothing is failing.

name.text: State change after writing production code

questiontext.text: You legally write production code that makes the failing test pass. How does the state change?

answer.text: The failing test is cleared, all tests are green, and the completed-cycle count increases by one

feedback.text: Correct — reaching green completes a red-green cycle.

answer.text: The failing test remains, but the cycle count still increases

feedback.text: No — passing the test clears the failing flag as part of reaching green.

answer.text: Nothing changes except a log entry

feedback.text: The state advances: failing cleared, all green, and one more completed cycle.

answer.text: The cycle count resets to zero

feedback.text: The count increases by one; it does not reset.

generalfeedback.text: Writing production code to pass the failing test moves you to green: the failing flag clears, all tests pass, and the completed-cycle count goes up by one, recording that a red-green cycle finished.

name.text: State change after writing a failing test

questiontext.text: From a green state you legally write a failing test. How does the state change?

answer.text: A test is now failing and the state is no longer all green

feedback.text: Correct — writing a failing test turns the state red.

answer.text: The completed-cycle count increases by one

feedback.text: The cycle count advances only when you reach green, not when you write a failing test.

answer.text: All tests remain green

feedback.text: No — a newly written failing test means the state is no longer all green.

answer.text: The state is unchanged

feedback.text: It changes: there is now a failing test and the state is red.

generalfeedback.text: Writing a failing test sets the failing flag and makes the state no longer all green (it turns red). The completed-cycle count does not change yet; that only advances when the test is made to pass.

name.text: Match the reason: refactor while red

questiontext.text: Which situation triggers the message "you may not refactor while a test is failing. Get to green first"?

answer.text: Attempting to refactor while a test is currently failing

feedback.text: Correct — this exact reason is shown for refactoring while red.

answer.text: Attempting to refactor at the very start with nothing written

feedback.text: That case shows "nothing to refactor yet", not "get to green first".

answer.text: Writing production code with no failing test

feedback.text: That shows the "write a failing test first" reason, a different message.

answer.text: Writing a second failing test

feedback.text: That shows "make it pass before writing another", a different message.

generalfeedback.text: The "get to green first" message is specific to trying to refactor while a test is failing. Refactoring before any cycle instead reports "nothing to refactor yet", so the two blocked-refactor cases have distinct reasons.

name.text: Match the reason: production code with no failing test

questiontext.text: Which situation triggers the message "you may not write production code without a failing test. Write a failing test first"?

answer.text: Trying to write production code when no test is failing

feedback.text: Correct — production code with nothing failing shows this exact reason.

answer.text: Trying to refactor while a test is failing

feedback.text: That shows "get to green first", a different message.

answer.text: Writing a second failing test

feedback.text: That shows "make it pass before writing another", a different message.

answer.text: Trying to refactor at the very start with nothing written

feedback.text: That shows "nothing to refactor yet", a different message.

generalfeedback.text: The "write a failing test first" message is specific to attempting production code when no test is failing. Each blocked action has its own reason: refactoring while red reports "get to green first", a second failing test reports "make it pass before writing another", and refactoring before any cycle reports "nothing to refactor yet".

name.text: Why illegal moves are blocked

questiontext.text: Why does the explorer block illegal moves instead of just letting them happen?

answer.text: To enforce the TDD discipline and teach the rules by naming the one each blocked move would break

feedback.text: Correct — blocking plus an explanation is how it teaches the discipline.

answer.text: To make the exercise slower on purpose

feedback.text: The purpose is to enforce and explain the rules, not to slow you down.

answer.text: Because the underlying tools cannot run those actions

feedback.text: The block is a deliberate teaching of discipline, not a technical limitation.

answer.text: To hide the current state from the learner

feedback.text: The state stays visible; blocking a move explains which rule it would break.

generalfeedback.text: By blocking an illegal move and naming the violated rule, the explorer makes the TDD discipline concrete: you experience exactly which rule each mis-step breaks, rather than only reading about it.

name.text: Why the rules yield high coverage

questiontext.text: Why does the rule "no production code without a failing test" tend to produce high test coverage?

answer.text: Because every piece of production code is written to satisfy some test, the behaviour is covered by construction

feedback.text: Correct — code only exists to pass a test, so tests exercise it by design.

answer.text: Because the explorer counts coverage automatically

feedback.text: Coverage is a side effect of the rule, not something the explorer measures.

answer.text: Because tests are added after the code to reach a target percentage

feedback.text: Tests come first here; coverage follows from code only existing to pass a test.

answer.text: Because refactoring adds new tests

feedback.text: Refactoring preserves behaviour and does not add tests; coverage comes from the test-first rule.

generalfeedback.text: If code may only be written to pass a failing test, then every behaviour that made it into the code was demanded by a test. Coverage therefore arises by construction rather than being chased after the fact.

name.text: Why small steps give fast feedback

questiontext.text: Why does allowing only one failing test at a time produce fast feedback on defects?

answer.text: Each step is tiny, so when something breaks, the failure points to the last small change

feedback.text: Correct — small increments make defects easy to localise.

answer.text: Because tests run on a faster machine

feedback.text: Feedback speed here is about small steps, not hardware.

answer.text: Because many failing tests are debugged together

feedback.text: The rule forbids many failing tests at once; single steps are what localise failures.

answer.text: Because production code is written before the test

feedback.text: The test comes first; the fast feedback comes from tiny one-at-a-time steps.

generalfeedback.text: Because you advance one small failing test at a time, a new failure almost always traces to the last tiny change. That tight loop makes diagnosis quick, which is a core benefit of the discipline.

name.text: Why the rules keep code minimal

questiontext.text: How does requiring a failing test before production code keep the codebase minimal?

answer.text: Code is added only to pass a specific failing test, so there is no speculative, unrequested code

feedback.text: Correct — every line answers a test, discouraging gold-plating.

answer.text: The explorer deletes any code above a size limit

feedback.text: There is no size limit; minimalism comes from code only existing to pass a test.

answer.text: It bans refactoring, so code never grows

feedback.text: Refactoring is allowed from green; minimalism comes from the test-first rule.

answer.text: It requires deleting a test for every line added

feedback.text: No such rule exists; code stays minimal because each piece must pass a failing test.

generalfeedback.text: Since production code is authorised only by a failing test, code written "just in case" has no justification and is forbidden. The discipline therefore pushes toward minimal, demand-driven code rather than speculative additions.

name.text: What the refactor action reveals about refactoring

questiontext.text: In the model, the refactor action changes only the phase; it does not clear a failing test, change "all green", or increment the cycle count. What does this reflect about refactoring in TDD?

answer.text: Refactoring changes structure, not behaviour — the tests stay green throughout

feedback.text: Correct — a behaviour-preserving step leaves the test status untouched.

answer.text: Refactoring completes a new red-green cycle

feedback.text: No — the cycle count does not change; refactoring is not a red-green cycle.

answer.text: Refactoring introduces a new failing test

feedback.text: It leaves the failing flag untouched; refactoring must keep tests green.

answer.text: Refactoring turns the state red so you can add code

feedback.text: Refactoring stays green; you do not go red to refactor.

generalfeedback.text: Because refactor leaves the test flags and cycle count unchanged, the model captures that refactoring is behaviour-preserving: you improve structure while all tests remain green, so no new failing test appears and no cycle is completed.

name.text: Why "all green" is true at the start

questiontext.text: The explorer reports All green = true at the very start, before any test exists. Why?

answer.text: It is vacuously true — with no tests written, none is failing

feedback.text: Correct — no failing tests means the "all pass" condition holds trivially.

answer.text: Because a hidden passing test is created at startup

feedback.text: No hidden test exists; the flag is vacuously true because nothing is failing.

answer.text: Because the first cycle has already completed

feedback.text: No cycle is complete at the start; the flag is simply vacuously true.

answer.text: Because the production code compiled

feedback.text: It is about test status, not compilation; with no tests, none fails.

generalfeedback.text: "All green" means every written test passes. When no test has been written, that condition is vacuously satisfied. This is why refactoring still needs a completed cycle: green alone is not enough, because green can hold trivially.

name.text: Which action increments the cycle count

questiontext.text: Which action increments the completed-cycle count?

answer.text: Writing production code that takes the failing test to passing (reaching green)

feedback.text: Correct — completing red-to-green is what advances the count.

answer.text: Writing a failing test

feedback.text: Writing a failing test turns the state red; it does not complete a cycle.

answer.text: Refactoring

feedback.text: Refactoring preserves behaviour and leaves the count unchanged.

answer.text: Resetting the explorer

feedback.text: Resetting returns to the initial state; it does not complete a cycle.

generalfeedback.text: The completed-cycle count advances only when production code makes the failing test pass, i.e. when a red-green cycle finishes. Writing a failing test and refactoring both leave the count unchanged.

name.text: Interpreting the explorer's self-check

questiontext.text: The explorer's built-in self-check asks which action is always illegal in strict TDD. What is the answer, and why?

answer.text: Writing production code before any failing test exists — you must never write production code without a failing test to justify it

feedback.text: Correct — that is the first and most important rule.

answer.text: Writing a failing test when all tests pass — because tests should never change once green

feedback.text: That is legal; a new failing test starts the next cycle from green.

answer.text: Refactoring after achieving green — because green code must never be touched

feedback.text: Refactoring from green is legal and encouraged; it is not the illegal action.

answer.text: Writing production code when there is a failing test — because tests block code

feedback.text: That is exactly the legal case: production code is written to pass a failing test.

generalfeedback.text: The self-check's answer is that writing production code before any failing test exists is always illegal. That reflects the governing rule: never write production code without a failing test to justify it.

name.text: Green but nothing to refactor

questiontext.text: At the start, all tests are green, yet refactoring is still blocked. Why does green alone not permit a refactor?

answer.text: Because no red-green cycle is complete yet, so no code has been produced to refactor

feedback.text: Correct — refactoring also requires at least one completed cycle.

answer.text: Because green at the start actually means a test is failing

feedback.text: No — green means nothing is failing; the block is that no cycle is complete.

answer.text: Because refactoring requires two completed cycles

feedback.text: One completed cycle is enough; the start simply has none.

answer.text: Because the reset button must be pressed first

feedback.text: Reset is unrelated; refactoring needs a completed cycle, which the start lacks.

generalfeedback.text: Refactoring requires green and at least one completed red-green cycle. At the start green holds vacuously but no cycle is complete, so there is nothing built to clean up and the move is blocked with "nothing to refactor yet."

name.text: Why the rules build a safety net

questiontext.text: How do these rules build a regression safety net over time?

answer.text: Tests are written before the code and always brought back to green, so a growing suite guards against later breakages

feedback.text: Correct — the accumulating green suite is the safety net.

answer.text: The explorer keeps a backup copy of the code after each move

feedback.text: The safety net is the test suite, not code backups.

answer.text: Refactoring deletes old tests to keep the suite small

feedback.text: Tests are kept and stay green; deleting them would remove the safety net.

answer.text: Production code is never changed once written

feedback.text: Code is changed and refactored; the green suite is what catches regressions.

generalfeedback.text: Each cycle adds a test and drives it to green, so the suite grows steadily. Because you always return to green, that accumulating suite will fail if a later change breaks earlier behaviour — a regression safety net produced by following the rules.

name.text: Edge: two refactors in a row

questiontext.text: After one completed cycle you refactor, then try to refactor again immediately. Is the second refactor legal?

answer.text: Yes — the tests are still green and a cycle is already complete, so refactoring remains legal

feedback.text: Correct — refactoring does not consume the green state or the completed cycle.

answer.text: No — you may refactor only once per cycle

feedback.text: There is no once-per-cycle limit; the conditions still hold, so it is legal.

answer.text: No — the first refactor turned the state red

feedback.text: Refactoring keeps the state green; it does not go red.

answer.text: Only if you write a failing test in between

feedback.text: No new test is required; green plus a completed cycle already permits refactoring.

generalfeedback.text: Refactoring leaves the state green and the completed-cycle count unchanged, so the refactoring conditions still hold afterwards. A second consecutive refactor is therefore legal.

name.text: Mapping the production-code rule to Uncle Bob's laws

questiontext.text: The rule behind the message "you may not write production code without a failing test" corresponds to which of Uncle Bob's Three Laws of TDD?

answer.text: The first law: write no production code except to make a failing test pass

feedback.text: Correct — this is the first law of TDD.

answer.text: The law that you must refactor after every test

feedback.text: Refactoring after green is part of the cycle, not the first law about production code.

answer.text: The law that tests must run in under a second

feedback.text: Test speed is a guideline, not the law this message reflects.

answer.text: The law that every method needs a test

feedback.text: The rule is about not writing code without a failing test, which is the first law.

generalfeedback.text: "You may not write production code without a failing test" is Uncle Bob's first law of TDD: write no production code except to make a failing test pass. The explorer enforces exactly this by blocking production code when nothing is failing.

name.text: Legal moves from green after one cycle

questiontext.text: After exactly one completed cycle, with all tests green and none failing (and no refactor yet), which actions are legal?

answer.text: Writing a new failing test or refactoring; writing production code is illegal

feedback.text: Correct — from green you may start a new test or refactor, but not write code with nothing failing.

answer.text: Only writing production code

feedback.text: Production code is the one blocked move here, since no test is failing.

answer.text: Only refactoring

feedback.text: Writing a new failing test is also legal from green.

answer.text: All three actions are legal

feedback.text: Writing production code is blocked because no test is failing.

generalfeedback.text: From green after a cycle, there is no failing test, so production code is blocked. Writing a new failing test (start the next cycle) and refactoring (green plus a completed cycle) are both legal.

name.text: Benefit of one failing test at a time

questiontext.text: The rules permit only one failing test at a time. What practical benefit does this give the moment a test goes red?

answer.text: You always know exactly which single expectation is unmet, so diagnosis is immediate

feedback.text: Correct — one red test pinpoints the unmet behaviour.

answer.text: You can ignore the red test until several accumulate

feedback.text: The rule forbids accumulating failing tests; you resolve the one red test now.

answer.text: You never have to run the test suite

feedback.text: You still run tests; the benefit is that a single red test is easy to interpret.

answer.text: The explorer fixes the test for you

feedback.text: It does not fix code; the benefit is a clear, single failing expectation.

generalfeedback.text: With at most one failing test, a red result identifies exactly which expectation is currently unmet. There is no ambiguity about which of several failures to chase, so you can diagnose and resolve it right away.

name.text: An illegal move leaves the state unchanged

questiontext.text: When a move is blocked as illegal, the explorer leaves the current state unchanged.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a blocked move does not advance the state; only the explanation is shown.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: An illegal move is refused and the state stays exactly as it was.

generalfeedback.text: A legal move advances the state; an illegal move is blocked, so the phase, failing-test flag, all-green flag, and cycle count all stay unchanged while the violated rule is explained. This lets you retry a different, legal action from the same state.

name.text: What the Rules Explorer captures versus the cycle

questiontext.text: How does the TDD Rules Explorer differ in focus from a red-green-refactor cycle walkthrough?

answer.text: It defines which actions are permitted in each state and why illegal ones are forbidden — the discipline, not just the phase sequence

feedback.text: Correct — the Rules Explorer is about legality and discipline.

answer.text: It only animates the colours red, green, and refactor with no rules

feedback.text: That is closer to a cycle walkthrough; the Rules Explorer enforces legality.

answer.text: It replaces tests with a coverage percentage

feedback.text: It does not deal in coverage; it enforces the discipline rules.

answer.text: It is only about naming the three phases in order

feedback.text: Naming the phases is the cycle view; the Rules Explorer is about which actions are legal and why.

generalfeedback.text: A cycle walkthrough shows the phases red, green, and refactor in sequence. The Rules Explorer instead enforces the discipline: from any state it decides which of the three actions are legal and, when one is not, explains exactly which rule that move would break.
